source.title_on_document: Leveraging LLMs for Design Ideation: An AI Tool to Assist Creativity

paper_design_summary: University students performed small-group design ideation with ALIA or in a control condition allowing internet resources; the allocation mechanism is not described. The main comparison reports participant feedback and self-ratings, while analysis of the ideas themselves is deferred to future work. Three earlier functionality pilots are mentioned collectively, without separately reported samples or quantitative outcomes.

studies.label: Main comparison of ALIA-assisted and control design ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Small-group sessions used ALIA or a control condition without ALIA, with internet resources permitted in the control condition. The paper describes the conditions but never explains how participants or groups entered them; the quoted sentence identifies conditions, not an allocation mechanism.
assignment.quote: The experiments were divided into two categories—the control group, i.e. without the intervention of ALIA, and the experimental group, i.e. using ALIA in ideation session.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3.5, Experiment Setup; no assignment mechanism is stated elsewhere in the full text.

arms.name: Experimental: ALIA-assisted ideation
arms.description: Six groups with two participants per group used ALIA as an assistive system (p. 6, Section 3.5). Analyzed-person count is left null: Figure 4 labels the experimental difficulty item as 12 responses and the idea-rating item as 13 responses, although the latter bars show counts 0, 1, 1, 9, 1 (p. 7, Figure 4).

arms.name: Control: ideation without ALIA
arms.description: Six groups, each with two participants except one group with three; no explicit ideation-method instructions, with internet resources permitted (p. 6, Section 3.5). Figure 4 labels each control item as 13 responses; the paper does not separately state a count of distinct people analyzed (p. 7, Figure 4).

participants.who: University students aged 18 to 20, described as fresher design undergraduates and somewhat familiar with brainstorming and ideation. Session membership is given by group composition in the quote, rather than an explicit total analyzed-person count. Figure 4 reports response counts and contains conflicting experimental denominators: the difficulty item says 12 responses, the idea-rating item says 13 responses, and the idea-rating bars show 0, 1, 1, 9, 1. Distinct people included in the reported idea-rating analysis cannot be confirmed; numeric analyzed-person counts are therefore null.
participants.quote: Both categories involved 6 different groups, where each group had 2 participants, with the exception of one control group, which had 3 participants.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 3.5 (group composition, ages, university students); p. 7, Figure 4 (response counts and conflicting experimental denominator) and Section 5 (fresher design undergraduates).

ai_tool.name_model: ALIA (Analogical LLM Ideation Agent), using Mistral 7b
ai_tool.how_used: Speech-to-text and summaries of group discussion supply context to an LLM, which displays starter questions, loosely related words, analogical questions, and thesis/antithesis questions as inspirational stimuli. Participants can control progression using a light-dependent resistor and may disregard unhelpful stimuli. See pp. 4-6, Sections 3.1-3.5; model named on p. 7, Section 5.

task.description: Small-group design ideation: each group received a different problem statement, and the same six problem statements were used across ALIA and control conditions. Sessions occurred in a closed, soundproofed room, with sticky notes available. Specific problem statements are not supplied (p. 6, Section 3.5).

outcomes.name: Self-rated quality of ideas: post-session question, How would you rate your ideas?
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Good self-ratings: experimental (ALIA) 9 (75%); control 5 (38.5%). Experimental idea-rating chart is labeled 13 responses, but its category counts are Poor 0, Bad 1, Okay 1, Good 9, Excellent 1; its other chart, for difficulty generating ideas, is labeled 12 responses. Control idea-rating chart is labeled 13 responses. These are participants' own post-session assessments, not independently scored idea quality. No inferential contrast is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Figure 4, right-hand control and experimental panels (idea ratings), and lower-left panel (experimental difficulty response count); p. 6, Section 4 (feedback source).

eligibility.reason: The main comparison names AI and control conditions but states neither random assignment nor another allocation mechanism (p. 6, Section 3.5), so criterion 1 is unclear and design_class is other. Its reported composition is six groups per condition, two people per group except one control group with three, which is below 50 people (p. 6, Section 3.5); the precise analyzed-person denominator is left null because only feedback-response counts are plotted and the experimental idea-rating header conflicts with its bars (p. 7, Figure 4). The paper explicitly limits its report to participants' reactions (p. 2, Section 1), uses post-session self-assessments (pp. 6-7, Section 4 and Figure 4), and defers novelty/idea-output analysis to future work (p. 7, Section 5; p. 8, Section 6). The three preliminary pilots report functionality feedback without participant counts or scored creative outputs (p. 5, Section 3.3). Self-report-only evidence does not qualify for core or a context class under the codebook.

one_line_finding: Participants rated their ideas good in 75% (9) of ALIA responses versus 38.5% (5) of control responses (p. 7, Figure 4); assignment is unstated, and no qualifying output-scored creativity outcome is reported.
